title: Gunnison County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gunnison County wells have a 70-foot median depth and 15 gpm median reported yield. Compare drilling costs, water levels and risks before buying.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Gunnison County
intro_html:
A shallow countywide median does not make every Gunnison County lot an easy drill. Recorded well depths center on 70 feet, but mountain bedrock can change the job sharply between neighboring properties. Start with nearby construction records, not just the county average.

Colorado DWR records include 8,832 permits across the county, with 5,210 recorded as constructed. Those records are a useful starting point for buying around Gunnison, Almont, Crested Butte or Pitkin, but a permit alone does not establish a working water supply.

sections.heading: A 70-Foot Median, With a Much Deeper Mountain Tail
sections.html:
Among the 5,407 wells reporting depth, the median is 70 feet and the middle half runs from 37 to 180 feet. That spread matters when comparing bids: a quote built around the median can fall short if your lot needs a deeper bore. Although 59% of reported depths are under 100 feet, the 90th percentile reaches 350 feet.

Permit aquifer labels are mostly unnamed or fractured bedrock; only 58 wells explicitly name Alluvial. Those labels do not prove the geology beneath a particular parcel. In fractured mountain rock, productive openings can be irregular. Compare nearby logs around Marble or Mount Crested Butte for terrain and formation, not merely proximity.

sections.heading: Gunnison County Yield Records Favor Usable Flows
sections.html:
The 15 gpm median reported yield is encouraging, and the middle half spans 7 to 15 gpm. But yields appear in only 1,992 records, so this is a picture of reporting wells rather than a guarantee for all permitted locations.

At the lower end, 1% report less than 1 gpm and 12% report 1–5 gpm. A buyer encountering a low-yield well should ask about sustained pumping, recovery and storage before accepting it as adequate. A brief completion test is not the same as reliable household performance. Also separate physical capacity from legal use: a productive well does not automatically come with permission to irrigate or supply additional buildings.

sections.heading: Water Often Stands Above the Bottom of the Well
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the total drilled depth. In Gunnison County, the 527 reporting records show a 27-foot median, with the middle half between 9 and 60 feet below ground. A bore may extend substantially deeper to reach water-bearing fractures and accommodate the pump.

The decade medians do not show a steady countywide decline: they move from 45 feet in the 1970s to 18 in the 1980s, 22 in the 1990s, 16 in the 2000s, 30 in the 2010s and 27 in the 2020s. These are different groups of measurements, not continuous monitoring of the same wells. Ask for current static and pumping levels on the property itself.

sections.heading: The County's Permit History Peaks in the 1990s
sections.html:
The busiest listed permit decade was the 1990s, with 2,100 permits, followed by 1,501 in the 2000s. Records list 837 in the 2010s and 544 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, and issuance does not establish when a well was actually drilled.

Bob Williams Drilling Co. (Williams, Robert F.) leads the listed drilling records with 3,340 entries; Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) has 253. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 76% of permits, but monitoring accounts for 11%. Check the use and construction documents before treating a nearby map point as a comparable household well.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Borehole in Gunnison County
sections.html:
The supplied drilling model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65–$100 per foot. At the county's 70-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $4,600–$7,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $10,600–$19,000.

Treat that as a planning allowance, not a parcel quote. The 37–180-foot middle depth range leaves substantial room for a different drilling bill. Ask the driller to spell out casing, grout, difficult-ground charges and what happens if the bore produces too little water. On a mountain building site, rig access and the route from the well to the house also need review before settling the budget.

sections.heading: Mine History and Water Testing Deserve a Close Look
sections.html:
The environmental inventory lists 13 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 360 historic mine features and 6 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles of the mapped area. These are screening flags, not evidence that every nearby well is contaminated. A sampling location is not necessarily a confirmed contamination source.

Before buying, obtain laboratory testing for drinking-water quality and ask local health officials which additional tests fit the property's mine history or mapped environmental concerns. Review casing, grout, drainage and septic placement as well. Low-yield records also warrant caution, but the supplied data do not establish a dry-hole rate. Neither a nearby producing well nor an issued permit guarantees success on an undrilled lot.

sections.heading: Buying in Almont or Building Near Somerset
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and match it to the well actually serving the property. Confirm allowed uses, construction details and any conditions before assuming household permission covers livestock, irrigation or another dwelling. Exempt household-use wells have restrictions, and some proposed uses may require augmentation in an over-appropriated basin.

For a lot in Almont, Somerset or Crested Butte, compare neighboring wells in similar terrain, then have the driller review access and the proposed location. Coordinate the well with septic suitability, required separation, the driveway and the building footprint. For an existing home, request a pumping and recovery assessment, current water testing and repair records before making the purchase contingent on a dependable supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gunnison County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 70 feet, and the middle half of wells runs from 37 to 180 feet. Although 59% are under 100 feet, the 90th percentile reaches 350 feet. Mountain fractures make individual results variable, so nearby construction logs are more useful for a parcel estimate than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Gunnison County?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 70-foot median depth, the hole is about $4,600–$7,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $10,600–$19,000. Get a parcel-specific quote that addresses depth uncertainty, casing, access and inadequate production.

faq.q: How much water do Gunnison County wells produce?
faq.a: Among 1,992 records reporting pump yield, the median is 15 gpm and the middle half is 7–15 gpm. However, 1% report under 1 gpm and 12% report 1–5 gpm. For a purchase, verify sustained output and recovery rather than relying solely on the yield recorded when the well was completed.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Gunnison County?
faq.a: Safety requires testing the individual well. The mapped environmental inventory includes 13 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 360 historic mine features and 6 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles of the mapped area. Those counts do not establish contamination at your property. Request drinking-water testing and locally appropriate testing for nearby environmental concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Gunnison County?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a steady decline. Median depth to water was 45 feet in the 1970s, 16 feet in the 2000s, 30 feet in the 2010s and 27 feet in the 2020s. Because these are different measurement groups, use current property-level water levels and pumping performance to assess a particular well.
